title: Where things live in memory during boot

steps.title: Two memories: a tiny on-chip one and the big DDR
steps.body:
Boot uses two address ranges. On the left is SYSRAM, 256 KiB of on-chip RAM from `0x0E000000`, which works from power-on and holds BL2 and BL31. On the right is the 4 GiB of LPDDR4 starting at `0x8000_0000`, which only works after BL2 trains it.

Each card gives a name, its start address and why that address was chosen. The DDR side is not drawn to scale.

steps.title: BL2 runs from SYSRAM at 0x0E017000
steps.body:
In this build BL2 occupies `0x0E017000` to `0x0E02CFE8`, about 90 KB of code and data. The Boot ROM first copies the `.stm32` payload (174,568 bytes) to `0x0E002600` and jumps in.

BL2 is the stage that makes DDR usable, so it has to live in memory that already works.

steps.title: BL2 carries its own small device tree
steps.body:
A DTB (compiled device tree, a description of the hardware) of 24 KiB is reserved at `0x0E011000`. It tells BL2 about clocks, DDR and which storage to read.

This is BL2's own file, separate from U-Boot's and the kernel's.

steps.title: The DDR training code sits in SRAM1 first
steps.body:
`lpddr4_pmu_train.bin` is copied to `0x0E040000` and then loaded into the DDR PHY (the circuit that talks to the memory chips), per `STM32MP_DDR_FW_BASE`.

It must go through on-chip RAM because DDR is exactly what is not working yet.

steps.title: BL31 owns the bottom of SYSRAM for good
steps.body:
BL31 is loaded at `0x0E000000`, the start of SYSRAM, with 92 KiB left for it below BL2 (`STM32MP_BL31_SIZE`). While BL2 runs, `fw-config` (its load plan) is also read to the same start address.

BL31 stays here for the whole life of the system.

steps.title: OP-TEE gets 32 MiB of DDR that Linux must not touch
steps.body:
OP-TEE sits at `0x82000000`, 32 MiB (`CFG_TZDRAM_START` and size `0x02000000`), marked secure and firewalled by RISAF (a hardware memory firewall).

The kernel device tree also reserves `fw@80000000`, 64 MiB with `no-map`, so Linux never uses `0x80000000` to `0x83FFFFFF`. That range covers OP-TEE.

steps.title: U-Boot and its device tree are loaded next to each other
steps.body:
`u-boot-nodtb.bin` is loaded at `0x84000000`, up to 4 MiB (`STM32MP_BL33_MAX_SIZE`). U-Boot then relocates itself to the top of DDR, and `0x84000000` is also `kernel_comp_addr_r`.

BL2 puts `u-boot.dtb` at `0x84400000` (up to 256 KiB), which U-Boot reads at start.

steps.title: U-Boot picks load addresses for the kernel; Linux gets the rest
steps.body:
U-Boot loads the `Image` at `0x8A000000` and the DTB at `0x90000000` (`fdt_addr_r`). The script goes to `0x90100000`, the `extlinux.conf` text to `0x90200000`, overlays to `0x90300000` and a ramdisk to `0x90400000`.

After `booti` the kernel runs from here and owns all DDR that is not reserved.

steps.title: Takeaway: every address traces to one definition
steps.body:
`DDR_BASE` is `0x80000000`. `BL33_BASE` is `DDR_BASE + 0x04000000 = 0x84000000` with `BL33_MAX_SIZE` `0x400000`, and `HW_CONFIG_BASE` follows at `0x84400000`.

OP-TEE's address comes from `fdts/stm32mp257f-dk-ca35tdcid-fw-config.dtsi`. `BL33_BASE` and `HW_CONFIG_BASE` are computed from `DDR_BASE`, so they follow it.
